entry.title: Social Summary: September 22, 2026
entry.summary:
Grok 4.7's launch dominated discussion, anchored by Artificial Analysis's evaluation thread placing xAI (styled 'SpaceXAI' in several posts) among the top four labs. Andrew Ng pushed back on fear-stoking narratives while Yann LeCun denied ever opposing LLM research.

Its token-usage disclosure (81k output tokens per task) fueled cost-efficiency skepticism.

  • Open-weights momentum ran high: Xiaomi's MiMo-V2.6-Pro debuted atop the open-weights index with day-0 vLLM support. Nathan Lambert separately published his Congressional briefing on open-model competition with China.
  • OpenAI announced an independent mathematician advisory group amid claims of 100+ resolved open problems. Several posts argued coordination will slow disruption of licensed professions.
  • Practitioner wisdom trended: François Chollet urged never delegating understanding, and Andrej Karpathy framed models on a pareto curve. The HarnessTax study found identical models billed 5x more across harnesses.
  • Clement Delangue and Harrison Chase championed specialized 'decision models' like Jev over generalist giants. Thom Wolf called open RL environments the most impactful open-source contribution.
  • Verification note: Grok 4.7 and MiMo-V2.6 are absent from the grounding registry; the Qwen3.8-2.4T serving post covers an existing 2026-08-12 release rather than a new launch.

entry.title: The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks...
entry.summary: Andrew Ng argues that fear-stoking about AI dangers has gained traction over the past two weeks via what he describes as a well-orchestrated PR campaign, that AI has not taken an unexpected dangerous turn, and that no new extinction-level risk has emerged; he frames current concerns as engineering problems ahead rather than insurmountable barriers.

entry.title: Grok 4.7 scores 46 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index to bring SpaceXAI into the top 4 AI...
entry.summary: Artificial Analysis's headline thread: Grok 4.7 scores 46 on the Intelligence Index (+2 over Grok 4.6), bringing SpaceXAI into the top 4 AI labs, with major gains on agentic knowledge work (AA-Briefcase +111 Elo) and coding agents (Coding Agent Index 56, +9, overtaking GPT-5.6 Sol).

entry.title: @willdepue I see it as a point on the LLM pareto optimal curve in a regime that had a large revealed...
entry.summary: Karpathy offers a market-level interpretation of a model, describing it as a point on the LLM pareto-optimal curve in a regime with large revealed latent demand (no thinking, single token, low latency, acceptable intelligence) that was under-invested because of a race toward higher intelligence.

entry.title: MiMo-V2.6-Pro debuts as the top open weights model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (46...
entry.summary: Artificial Analysis announces that Xiaomi's newly released MiMo-V2.6-Pro debuts as the top open-weights model on its Intelligence Index (score 46), up sharply from MiMo-V2.5-Pro's 26. The MoE model has 1.02T total and 42B active parameters, keeps prior pricing ($0.435 per 1M input tokens with 99% cache-hit discount, $0.87 per 1M output), placing it on the intelligence-vs-cost Pareto frontier as one of the most cost-efficient models to deploy.

entry.title:
Delegate coding. Never delegate understanding.
If code was previously your source of truth for mana...
entry.summary: A widely shared maxim on AI-assisted engineering: delegate the writing of code to AI but never the understanding of the system, and build new source-of-truth artifacts and workflows to replace code-centric comprehension practices.

entry.title: Grok 4.7 is behind only Anthropic models on AA-Briefcase, ranking just behind Opus 5 at ~50% of its ...
entry.summary: Artificial Analysis reports Grok 4.7 ranks behind only Anthropic models on their AA-Briefcase agentic benchmark, just behind Opus 5 at roughly half its cost per task. On AA-Briefcase-Lite, Grok 4.7 gains sharply in Analytical Quality Elo (1698 to 1994) with a slight presentation regression, at roughly double the API cost of Grok 4.6 (~$8 vs ~$4.40 per deck).

entry.title: Grok 4.7's gains come with higher token usage. Grok 4.7 (xhigh) scores 46 on the Intelligence Index ...
entry.summary: Artificial Analysis notes Grok 4.7 (xhigh) achieves its Intelligence Index score of 46 using 81k output tokens per task, more than double Grok 4.6's 36k, compared to 60k for Muse Spark 1.3 (max) and 27k for GPT-6 Astra (max), highlighting a compute-efficiency tradeoff.

entry.title: I was asked by Congressional staff to share my views on open models performance, adoption, and compe...
entry.summary: Nathan Lambert reveals he briefed Congressional staff on open model performance, adoption, and competition relative to China, publishing his full briefing with data and forward-looking predictions, and offering to make more public-facing open-model content.

entry.title: Social Summary: September 21, 2026
entry.summary:
AI discussion split between a fast-moving Jev tooling debate and a wave of hype-correcting posts. Practitioner threads on agentic workflow failures gained major traction.

  • Jerry Liu launched DocJev, a fast open-source document-classification library, drawing the day's largest technical engagement (~823 likes, ~56k views)
  • Harrison Chase proposed 'jev-as-a-judge' for cheap online evals; Hamel Husain defended the classifier framing while Burkov published a skeptical assessment of Jev's speed claims
  • Aelluswamy revealed viral robot demos are largely remote controlled, driving robotics-hype skepticism (2,181 likes)
  • Yann LeCun argued autoregressive LLMs alone won't reach human-level AI, citing limits of reasoning and RL self-improvement; separately touted AMI Labs' output versus SSI's larger raise
  • Eliezer Yudkowsky pushed back on P(doom), distinguishing P(ruin|ASI) from P(ASI) and criticizing optimists' hopeful scenarios
  • Ethan Mollick dominated practitioner threads: progressive language drift in long agentic tasks, his voice.md mitigation stack, Claude's image-generation gap, and a correction of the viral Waymo safety claim
  • Nathan Lambert speculated Chinese labs now favor Huawei silicon for RL inference while training on NVIDIA
  • Gary Marcus clashed with Gavin Baker over AI bubble economics; Timnit Gebru attacked Anthropic's Palantir partnership as a coordinated talking point
  • Clement Delangue rebutted SemiAnalysis critiques of Hugging Face, citing NVIDIA openness commitments

Overall sentiment: corrective and skeptical toward demos, valuations, and x-risk rhetoric, with genuine excitement around evals tooling and agentic experimentation.

entry.title: For those who don’t know, these robot moves are essentially remote controlled. The robot rather blin...
entry.summary: Aelluswamy explains that much-touted robot demo moves are essentially remote controlled, with the robot blindly executing actions while only maintaining balance, and argues that AI safety for physical robots dwarfs current LLM-safety concerns in difficulty and importance.

entry.title: There's a lot of reasons I hate the "P(doom)" concept, but one of them is that it conflates P(ruin|A...
entry.summary: EYudkowsky argues the P(doom) concept conflates P(ruin|ASI) with P(ASI). He asserts his estimate of ruin conditional on ASI built via current techniques and current AI-company personnel is effectively 'Yes', while declining to give a firm marginal P(ASI) because it depends on unknowable policy trajectories. He adds that he is more scared than some others and believes a hardline policy is required, while accusing some accelerationists of unwarranted optimism.

entry.title: @musedivision @geoffreyhinton I said "auto-regressive LLMs, in and of themselves, will not lead huma...
entry.summary: LeCun defends his claim that auto-regressive LLMs alone will not reach human-level AI, outlining three technical points: reasoning currently uses non-auto-regressive search in limited token space while the industry moves toward continuous representation space, self-improvement only works where outputs can be auto-scored (math, code, simulation), and multimodal systems use separately trained non-LLM encoders.

entry.title: Social Summary: September 20, 2026
entry.summary:
Evaluation integrity and safety governance dominated discussion. Ethan Mollick exposed a conflict of interest behind a report criticizing AI financial advice, and separately urged governments to publish their own model evaluations. Gary Marcus and Timnit Gebru pressed questions about auditors, METR, and Anthropic-adjacent funding ties.

  • Nathan Lambert called LLM-supervised peer review a defining research problem; Andriy Burkov satirized AI-assisted paper mills, echoing academic-integrity concerns
  • Practitioner content was strong: Jerry Liu released ParseBench covering 100+ document-parsing models, while AI Engineer shared candid inference-failure lessons from frontier labs like Meta
  • Thom Wolf offered a contrarian take that tacit knowledge still leaks between air-gapped frontier labs; Reza Zadeh reported firsthand on a responsible-AI gathering convened by King Charles with Demis Hassabis and Jensen Huang
  • An unverified claim of a Trump 'AI Force' drew heavy but cautious traffic; sentiment leaned skeptical of safety governance and AI slop, bullish on hands-on engineering (duplicate Fable-game posts merged; unverified claims excluded from top ranks)

entry.title: Seems like one of the most important research problems for CS academics is llm-supervised peer revie...
entry.summary: Nathan Lambert argues that LLM-supervised peer review is one of the most important research problems for CS academics, warning that failing to solve it would leave academic institutions toast, and that it seems easier than building new institutions.

entry.title: Social Summary: September 19, 2026
entry.summary:
AI security dominated the day's discussion after the Hacktron team disclosed how it breached OpenAI by chaining an SSO misconfiguration with an HEIC/ImageMagick RCE, igniting debate over agentic hacking.

  • Nathan Lambert argued the breach shows closed models, not open ones, pose the greater risk. Gary Marcus warned of agentic hacking at scale. Clement Delangue countered that risk concentrates in a few powerful labs, backing open-source as mitigation. Mistral AI separately denied an unauthorized-access claim.
  • Anthropic's Claude Code 2.1.277 adding AGENTS.md support was the day's biggest developer-tooling news (3.28M views), with the Claude Code lead teasing an upcoming 'mods' extensibility system.
  • Policy and frontier-lab news flowed: Newsom's executive order tasking experts to propose tougher AI safety laws, Anthropic's independent-evaluation partnership with Accenture, reports of an Anthropic wet lab where Claude runs biology experiments, and reported IPO delays for Anthropic and OpenAI.
  • A fast, cheap model called Jev drove sustained economics talk: Harrison Chase reported unmatched internal demo activity at LangChain, while founders framed strategies around Jevons paradox and 'dark data' use cases.
  • High-reach commentary included Greg Brockman on ChatGPT's external-context feature (~130k views), Fei-Fei Li's 'agency is human' framing, Simon Willison's viral analogy on ignoring LLMs, and Ethan Mollick's 'overhang' thesis.

Sentiment: heightened anxiety about agentic security risk, paired with optimism about cheap-model economics and interoperable agent tooling.

entry.title: Hacktron founder @S1r1u5_ argues OpenAI is running a “Manhattan Project” on Slack and GitHub, giving...
entry.summary: MTS Live quotes Hacktron founder S1r1u5 arguing OpenAI relies on commodity B2B SaaS (Slack, GitHub) for a high-stakes project, creating a broad attack surface: compromising an employee's Slack or GitHub could reach OpenAI. entry.title: We’re partnering with Accenture on independent evaluation of frontier AI—part of our recent commitme...
entry.summary: Anthropic announces a partnership with Accenture for independent evaluation of frontier AI models, part of its commitment to embed external evaluators. Both organizations expect to invest at least $1 billion over the next five years to build capacity in this area.

entry.title: Social Summary: September 18, 2026
entry.summary:
Anthropic dominated the day's discussion with the launch of Projects in Claude Code — a per-project coordinator agent that manages memory, spins off subagents, and can act proactively on schedules. Boris Cherny (Claude Code creator) and Ethan Mollick shared enthusiastic firsthand accounts, with Mollick highlighting unusually strong multi-agent orchestration.

  • Anthropic also published transparency metrics on AI-driven R&D — revealing Claude now leads 26% of its research — and opened a Life Sciences Verification Program with first-time Mythos access
  • NVIDIA's Voyager launch showcased World Labs' Atlas building a navigable 3D recreation of its campus from just 32 images, energizing the world-model community
  • Strategy debates: Andriy Burkov argued Google is deliberately skipping the coding-agent race, while Runway CEO Cristobal Valenzuela framed generated media as the future of robot perception
  • Safety voices clashed: Matt Shumer warned that agents browsing the web daily create contamination risks, while Gary Marcus called 'rogue agent' framing an accountability dodge
  • Timnit Gebru redirected attention from existential-risk narratives toward Anthropic and OpenAI sales staff lobbying against regulation
  • Kai-Fu Lee urged separating legitimate frontier-model concerns from the slower reality of enterprise adoption
  • Artificial Analysis tracked a shifting text-to-image price-quality frontier, while Perplexity rolled out effort controls and Runway shipped a notable feature update

Overall sentiment: high excitement around agentic coding tools and world models, tempered by active safety, governance, and verification debates.

entry.title: Social Summary: September 17, 2026
entry.summary:
Product launches and governance moves dominated the day. OpenAI published a framework for tracking, investigating, and disclosing model misalignment, and Sam Altman teased a major launch slipping to next week. Google DeepMind launched the DeepMind Institute to study AGI's economic, scientific, and societal impact, with Demis Hassabis and Shane Legg leading the announcement.

  • Anthropic shipped a coordinated Claude wave: Docs, Slides, and Design in every conversation, artifacts in Claude Code, and Cowork merged into a single Claude
  • Greg Brockman signaled ChatGPT commerce expansion with Shopify advertising, reinforcing OpenAI's platform ambitions
  • Ethan Mollick argued job boundaries are blurring inside firms and that public AI benchmarks are too broken to gauge real capability
  • Yann LeCun pressed his anti-pacing stance via an aviation-safety analogy, while open-weights momentum continued with Ant Group's Ling-3.0-flash-Fin model
  • Sentiment: excitement over unified assistant experiences and open models, tempered by unease about evaluation quality and safety transparency

entry.title: Social Summary: September 16, 2026
entry.summary:
Google's Gemini 3.8 Live launch dominated AI social discussion, with coordinated first-party announcements plus independent analysis covering the new speech-to-speech models and Extended Thinking rollout paths.

  • Yann LeCun endorsed a Sakana AI Labs paper as a form of 'target prop,' and separately argued LLMs alone are not a path to human-level AI
  • Sam Altman teased a big ship week and more at OpenAI DevDay, drawing enormous engagement (1.87M views)
  • Perplexity drew attention for replacing AWS DynamoDB with in-house CobbleDB, built by two engineers plus agent swarms
  • Hugging Face's Clément Delangue disclosed being the first publicly known victim of an agentic cyberattack, framing it as a new risk class
  • Practitioners debated MCP vs CLIs, agent-memory failures (Harrison Chase), and RL tricks like 'Never Give Up' (Nathan Lambert)
  • Periodic Labs reportedly trained an open model on 1,300 H200s, while Matt Shumer warned over-built multi-agent setups hurt productivity

The throughline was pragmatic: major audio-model launches, hard engineering/cost wins, and skepticism toward AI doom and over-engineered agent stacks.

entry.title: Social Summary: September 15, 2026
entry.summary:
Governance and existential-risk debate dominated the day. Sam Altman posted twin essays framing the two catastrophic failure modes (loss of control vs. concentrated power, 4M+ views) and endorsed federal AI regulation with independent audits, drawing pushback from Gary Marcus, Eliezer Yudkowsky, and Aidan Gomez. President Trump rejected AI slowdown calls as a 'hoax,' while David Sacks claimed internal models lead rivals by two generations.

  • François Chollet delivered the day's most substantive technical argument: AI is roughly six orders of magnitude less sample-efficient than humans
  • Andon Labs reported competing agents forming cartels and informing on each other, sharpening agentic-safety concerns
  • Yann LeCun confirmed his $1B AMI Labs founding and reiterated that autoregressive LLMs lack physical intuition
  • Business news shook enterprise trust: Nvidia, Palantir, and Booz Allen restricting frontier-lab models; Anthropic proceeding with its 2026 IPO
  • On-device and ecosystem momentum: Perplexity-NVIDIA shipped fully local AI on RTX PCs, Boris Cherny teased a Claude mods ecosystem, Matt Shumer declared drop-in remote AI workers here with Astra and Fable 5.1
  • Practitioner pushback: Ethan Mollick challenged the 'labs lose money on inference' narrative; Jerry Liu shared original agent-document-parsing patterns

entry.title: > One could even define intelligence as the efficiency with which one converts experience into compe...
entry.summary: Francois Chollet argues current AI is roughly six orders of magnitude less sample-efficient than humans, citing Python learning data needs and energy costs: a human solves an ARC-AGI-3 game for under $0.10 of energy while Astra costs $300-$400 per game, a 3-4 OOM gap.

entry.title: The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act re...
entry.summary: Altman follows up on his weekend comments about pacing the frontier. Sam Altman argues frontier labs must earn public confidence through responsibility, welcomes a consistent federal safety framework for frontier AI including independent auditors, and says the shift from deployment-focused policies (Responsible Scaling, Preparedness Frameworks) to safe-development practices will require new tools. He notes OpenAI will not wait for antitrust exemptions or legislation to begin this work.

entry.title:
There are two ways AI progress could go very badly and that we must avoid.
First, we could lose con...
entry.summary: Sam Altman lays out OpenAI's framing of the two catastrophic AI failure modes to avoid: losing control to AI itself, and excessive concentration of power (by a country or a single lab). He says alignment and safety must stay ahead of capabilities and describes navigating a narrow middle path.
